# The appointments Móði made — and who is keeping them

The mistake is reading myths as entertainment. Móði's cycle reads more like a charter — each story assigning a duty the modern world still pays for.

## At a Glance

- **Temple:** Móði
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Domain of influence:** Wrath, Son of Thor
- **Pattern seats:** 4
- **Sectors touched:** Commerce & Governance
- **Strongest seat:** Defense, Military & Security
- **Series:** The Resonance Files, No. 317 of 546

## The Cycle, Read Forward

### Defense, Military & Security — through *The Sons Who Survive*

The eddic poem Vafþrúðnismál asks the question every Norse listener cared about: who lives when the fire dies?  Óðinn, disguised as Gagnráðr, puts it to the all-wise giant: what of the gods survives Surtr's flames?

The atlas states the seat in one line: *Wrath embodied; the son who inherits the hammer and the fight.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. Industries do not invent their archetypes; they inherit them and call them best practice.

### Disaster Resilience & Recovery — through *The Lifting of Hrungnir*

After Þórr kills the giant Hrungnir in single combat at the ford, the giant's corpse falls across him, one leg pinning the thunder-god's neck to the ground.  The Æsir tug and heave in vain; none can shift the dead weight.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *He survives Ragnarök and inherits Mjöllnir; continuity after the end of everything.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. That is the cycle working: story becomes duty, duty becomes trade.

### Ancestry & Heritage Services — through *The Children of Þórr*

Snorri lists Þórr's children across his Edda, naming Móði and Magni as Þórr's sons by Járnsaxa, one of the giantesses (Gylfaginning; Skáldskaparmál 14), with the daughter Þrúðr among the children of Sif.  Their names are the point: Mag-ni, 'Might,' and Mó-ði, 'Wrath' — the two halves of the thunder-god's power personified as an inheritance.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *Through him Þórr's line does not end in the serpent's venom; the bloodline carried forward.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. That is the cycle working: story becomes duty, duty becomes trade.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The heir who takes up his father's hammer; succession as the thunder's doctrine.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. That is the cycle working: story becomes duty, duty becomes trade.

## The Theme That Runs the Cycle

Móði is not a god of independent myths. His entire dossier is a handful of verses: his name in a list of survivors, his place in a genealogy, and the skalds' habit of naming Þórr as his father. His significance lies in what he represents — the wrath that inherits the hammer — and in what his survival promises after Ragnarök.

## The Method, Stated Plainly

Skeptical? Good — the system is built for you. Every seat in this file carries its why-line and its weight, the full derivation is public at the [methodology page](/patterns/methodology/), and the challenge process is part of the design. Falsifiable is not a posture here; it is the mechanism.

## For the Ones Who Work There

If you work in defense, military & security, disaster resilience & recovery, or any trade this temple holds a seat in, this is the honest version of what a placement means: your industry beside the story it has been re-telling all along — on the temple floor itself, before an audience that came specifically to read it. The [patron tier](/modi/patron/) and the [advertising terms](/terms/advertising/) describe the mechanics; the resonance above describes the fit.
